newsitem.title: USA: GAO says still has many concerns about derivatives.
newsitem.headline: GAO says still has many concerns about derivatives.

text.p: The General Accounting Office, in an update to its controversial 1994 report on derivatives, said Friday that many of its concerns remain unaddressed.

"Although market participants, regulators and others have acted to improve the management, oversight and disclosure of derivatives risks, many of the concerns that GAO identified in its 1994 report still remain," the U.S. Congressional research arm wrote in its new report.
Market participants harshly criticized the 1994 report which called for additional federal regulation of derivatives.
After the release of the 1994 report, several investors and firms revealed massive losses from derivatives-related activities, GAO noted, including Orange County, California, and Barings Plc.

Partly as a result of those losses, banking and other regulators have initiated a host of measures to improve management of the risks involved in trading and investing with derivatives -- financial instruments whose value is based on the value of some other instrument, commodity or market index.
But the GAO warned that the measures might not be sufficient to avoid future problems.
"It is too soon to determine the effectiveness of many of the actions taken or proposed to date, and some of GAO's recommendations have yet to be fully implemented," GAO said.
For example, in its 1994 report, GAO called for accounting standards that would list all financial instruments, including derivatives, at market value.

In Friday's report, GAO renewed its support for market value accounting. But, it said, the latest draft proposal on derivatives accounting from the Financial Accounting Standards Board was a "significant step in the right direction."
"Serious shortcomings in accounting standards continue to be exposed as entities experience major losses for market-sensitive financial instruments, with seemingly little warning," the GAO said.

Market value accounting would give more warning, GAO said, but "it will take time to develop and gain acceptance for a new accounting model." The FASB proposal is "a reasonable interim accounting solution."
The GAO also sharply criticized a proposal by the Government Accounting Standards Board to reform accounting for U.S. municipalities.

"As state and local governmental entities are increasing their involvement with derivatives, it is essential that standards are developed to avoid inconsistent and potentially inappropriate accounting practices for these activities," GAO said. The latest GASB proposal does not address off-balance-sheet use of derivatives, it said.

The 165-page report also reiterated a call from the 1994 report for federal oversight of insurance company affiliates that deal in derivatives. Such affiliates "remain virtually unregulated," GAO said.

Weak corporate governance was the root cause of many derivatives losses over the past few years, the GAO said. While some voluntary measures have attempted to improve oversight and management of derivatives activities, more should be done, it concluded.

"Although these voluntary actions for improving corporate governance and controls are valuable, they may not be adopted by all of those who are vulnerable," the GAO said. "In addition, we continue to be concerned that favorable market conditions may mask the need for further improvements."
